fr:mainmatter.html:p: We find ourselves in-between LOVE and DDO. In particular, in DDO, they are concerned with learning a hierarchy of policies where the higher-level meta policy \eta must be usable online only given the current state.

html:ul.html:li: (+) The learned termination conditions \beta are dependent on the active skill.
(+) Exact inference \implies lower variance.
(-) Weak skill model \eta (z \mid s).
(-) No explicit encouragement for temporally-extended skills.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: On the contrary, in LOVE, they treat skills as a pure sequence-modeling problem. The posterior q_{\theta }(z_{t} \mid z_{t - 1}, b_{t}, x_{0}, \ldots , x_{T}) is purely used to label offline trajectories and give the skills meaning. To make them usable online, it is then required to learn an additional hierarchical policy over these skills.

html:ul.html:li: (+) The skill-labeler is allowed to use not only the current state but also the future visited states.
(+) Compression objective encourages temporally extended skills.
(-) Design inherently does not allow the terminations to be skill-dependent.
(-) Need to sample z's to compute gradients \implies higher-variance.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Our graphical model. We try to combine the desirable properties.

html:figure.html:figcaption: Each boundary depends on a skill and each skill depends on the whole sequence. Each boundary also depends on the whole history. However, the skill conditioned policy only requires the current state s and skill z. Thus, allowing the skills to be used.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We essentially combine the insight of LOVE where instead of trying to model the full joint distribution i.e. \mathbb {P}(\mathcal {H}, \xi ) we instead model \mathbb {P}(\mathcal {A}, \xi \mid \mathcal {S}), where we treat the entire state history as known.

In the language of HMMs, the emission probabilities only correspond to the actions. Therefore, we can perform the Forward-backward algorithm and condition on whatever component of the state we want without breaking the exactness.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. This is only a good idea for us because we do not need to use the meta controller during evaluation.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Deliberation cost. In LOVE, they encourage temporal extension through the compression loss. This requires an empirical approximation of the skillmarginal p(z). For me, this caused the skill entropy to just collapse to zero instead of encouraging temporally extended options. Instead, we use a deliberation cost more common in the options literature The Option-Critic Architecture, where we just add the switch-rate as an additional loss term.

html:ul.html:li: We are given the posterior \mathbb {P}(z_t = z, b_t = 1 \mid \mathcal {H}). In our implementation this would be (B, T, K)
We marginalize over skills z by summing to get \mathbb {P}(b_t = 1 \mid \mathcal {H})
Then average over batch B and time T to get expected reads.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: As in LOVE, we need to balance minimizing log-likelihood with compression / switching cost. To do so, we do dual descent.

html:ul.html:li: First, without compression, we run the algorithm and observe what is approximately the best attainable log-likelihood loss is.
Then, we minimize the deliberation cost subject to \mathcal {L}_{\text {likelihood}} \leq C + \epsilon
The skill network \eta (z_t \mid s_{0}, \ldots s_{T}) is a bidirectional GRU, where the hidden states are accumulated via running the GRU forwards and backwards and concatenating the results.
The termination network \beta (b_t \mid z_{t - 1}, s_{0}, \ldots , s_{t}) is a GRU, that only runs forward.
Instead of passing the previous skill as input, the output dimension is size K (number of skills).
The skill policy network \pi _{\theta }(a \mid s, z) is a standard Gaussian policy that take z as a one-hot encoding.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Setup. Assume we are given a set of skills \mathbf {z} \in \{0, \ldots , K\} along with a skill-conditioned lower-level policy \pi (s \mid z). Then what we want is to be able to learn the optimal goal-reaching policy over these skills. To do so, we must go beyond traditional offline skill-learning algorithms. We must Learn a value function over learned skills purely from offline data

Extending beyond pointmaze in locomotion. The main issue faced here is that our discriminator is too powerful in high dimensional state space. Namely, we score options based on their ability to reconstruct actions i.e. if \mathbb {P}(a_t \mid s_t, z_t = z) is high then we further increase the probability of selecting that option z. In higher-dimensional state spaces, the skill network \pi _{\theta }(a_t \cdot \mid s_t, z) is powerful enough to reconstruct a_t purely from s_t without using z. This basically provides no signal for which z to use, and we end up just selecting z uniformly every time step.

html:ul.html:li: I have seen a little sign of life from trying \pi (a \mid f_{\theta }(s), z) i.e. compressing s to a lower dimensional representation.
It may also be worth trying a really small network. Right now (256, 256) already gets very low reconstruction loss, so maybe we can go smaller?

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Conquering manipulation. In OGBench: Benchmarking Offline Goal-Conditioned RL, they provide a suite of manipulation environments in addition to the standard locomotion. One such environment, is the manipulation equivalent of the lights out game. This is a great test-bed to separate skill-learning from planning. In particular, the skill-learning portion can be clearly decomposed into the pressing of each of the buttons. However, when directly trying to use the LOVE it is not able to distinguish between these skills.

html:ul.html:li: On puzzle 3x3 LOVE terminates every 1.4 steps because all the skills look similar.
This is using the threshold \beta > 0.9.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pressing each of the buttons looks too similar, where the main discrepancy between them is only their termination condition. Since LOVE's termination condition is independent of skill, it is unable to distinguish between these.

html:ul.html:li: This is further confirmed in the scene environment. LOVE is able to distinguish between very different skills like open drawer vs. window. However, it is not able to distinguish between unlock drawer vs. window, where they only differ in pressing two adjacent buttons.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Injecting goals into the graphical model. Another failure mode of manipulation is that skills cannot be goal-independent. For example, in the generating policy of scene they have a pick and place skill that picks up the block and places it somewhere. Where to place the block is encoded in the goal. We can augment our graphical model to also allow the actions to depend on the goal.

html:figure.html:figcaption: Our graphical model with the goal included.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: However, we do not want the skills to become goal-conditioned policies. To get around this we can use the information bottleneck idea from InfoBot: Transfer and Exploration via the Information Bottleneck. Namely, we penalize the Mutual Information between the goal and action or goal and skill (TBD the right way to do this).
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Ideally, this would allow goal-dependent skills, where the goal is not the entire state space. For example, penalizing Mutual Information could cause just the desired block position as the information to be passed to the skill. This ignores the irrelavant components of the state space for that skill. Another skill may focus on whether the window is locked / unlocked, etc.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Get rid of weird threshold / turn into MPC-ish. Currently, when planning, we must tune the value_threshold for when we pass control to goal-conditioned policy. To get 89 percent on pointmaze we used -10. Instead of using a threshold, we could instead just treat the goal-conditioned policy as another skill. Furthermore, they could be seen as our primitive actions i.e. during planning we take the next state as the immediate next state instead of just jumping to goal (which would obv always be taken).

fr:frontmatter.fr:meta: @misc{farebrotherCompositionalPlanningJumpy2026, title = {Compositional {{Planning}} with {{Jumpy World Models}}}, author = {Farebrother, Jesse and Pirotta, Matteo and Tirinzoni, Andrea and Bellemare, Marc G. and Lazaric, Alessandro and Touati, Ahmed}, year = {2026}, doi = {10.48550/arXiv.2602.19634}, urldate = {2026-05-07}, number = {arXiv:2602.19634}, publisher = {arXiv}, file = {/home/kellen/Downloads/papers/Compositional Planning with Jumpy World Models - Farebrother et al..pdf}, keywords = {Computer Science - Artificial Intelligence,Computer Science - Machine Learning,Statistics - Machine Learning}, langid = {english}, archiveprefix = {arXiv}, abstract = {The ability to plan with temporal abstractions is central to intelligent decision-making. Rather than reasoning over primitive actions, we study agents that compose pre-trained policies as temporally extended actions, enabling solutions to complex tasks that no constituent alone can solve. Such compositional planning remains elusive as compounding errors in long-horizon predictions make it challenging to estimate the visitation distribution induced by sequencing policies. Motivated by the geometric policy composition framework introduced in arXiv:2206.08736, we address these challenges by learning predictive models of multi-step dynamics -- so-called jumpy world models -- that capture state occupancies induced by pre-trained policies across multiple timescales in an off-policy manner. Building on Temporal Difference Flows (arXiv:2503.09817), we enhance these models with a novel consistency objective that aligns predictions across timescales, improving long-horizon predictive accuracy. We further demonstrate how to combine these generative predictions to estimate the value of executing arbitrary sequences of policies over varying timescales. Empirically, we find that compositional planning with jumpy world models significantly improves zero-shot performance across a wide range of base policies on challenging manipulation and navigation tasks, yielding, on average, a 200\% relative improvement over planning with primitive actions on long-horizon tasks.}, primaryclass = {cs}, eprint = {2602.19634}, month = {February} }

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We find ourselves in-between LOVE and DDO. In particular, in DDO, they are concerned with learning a hierarchy of policies where the higher-level meta policy \eta must be usable online only given the current state.

(+) Compression objective encourages temporally extended skills.
(-) Design inherently does not allow the terminations to be skill-dependent.

In the language of HMMs, the emission probabilities only correspond to the actions. Therefore, we can perform the Forward-backward algorithm and condition on whatever component of the state we want without breaking the exactness.

For me, this caused the skill entropy to just collapse to zero instead of encouraging temporally extended options. The termination network \beta (b_t \mid z_{t - 1}, s_{0}, \ldots , s_{t}) is a GRU, that only runs forward.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Setup. Assume we are given a set of skills \mathbf {z} \in \{0, \ldots , K\} along with a skill-conditioned lower-level policy \pi (s \mid z). Then what we want is to be able to learn the optimal goal-reaching policy over these skills. To do so, we must go beyond traditional offline skill-learning algorithms. We must Learn a value function over learned skills purely from offline data

Extending beyond pointmaze in locomotion. The main issue faced here is that our discriminator is too powerful in high dimensional state space. Namely, we score options based on their ability to reconstruct actions i.e. if \mathbb {P}(a_t \mid s_t, z_t = z) is high then we further increase the probability of selecting that option z. In higher-dimensional state spaces, the skill network \pi _{\theta }(a_t \cdot \mid s_t, z) is powerful enough to reconstruct a_t purely from s_t without using z. This basically provides no signal for which z to use, and we end up just selecting z uniformly every time step.

html:ul.html:li: I have seen a little sign of life from trying \pi (a \mid f_{\theta }(s), z) i.e. compressing s to a lower dimensional representation.
It may also be worth trying a really small network. Right now (256, 256) already gets very low reconstruction loss, so maybe we can go smaller?

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Conquering manipulation. In OGBench: Benchmarking Offline Goal-Conditioned RL, they provide a suite of manipulation environments in addition to the standard locomotion. One such environment, is the manipulation equivalent of the lights out game. This is a great test-bed to separate skill-learning from planning. In particular, the skill-learning portion can be clearly decomposed into the pressing of each of the buttons. However, when directly trying to use the LOVE it is not able to distinguish between these skills.

html:ul.html:li: On puzzle 3x3 LOVE terminates every 1.4 steps because all the skills look similar.
This is using the threshold \beta > 0.9.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pressing each of the buttons looks too similar, where the main discrepancy between them is only their termination condition. Since LOVE's termination condition is independent of skill, it is unable to distinguish between these.

html:ul.html:li: This is further confirmed in the scene environment. LOVE is able to distinguish between very different skills like open drawer vs. window. However, it is not able to distinguish between unlock drawer vs. window, where they only differ in pressing two adjacent buttons.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Injecting goals into the graphical model. Another failure mode of manipulation is that skills cannot be goal-independent. For example, in the generating policy of scene they have a pick and place skill that picks up the block and places it somewhere. Where to place the block is encoded in the goal. We can augment our graphical model to also allow the actions to depend on the goal.

html:figure.html:figcaption: Our graphical model with the goal included.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: However, we do not want the skills to become goal-conditioned policies. To get around this we can use the information bottleneck idea from InfoBot: Transfer and Exploration via the Information Bottleneck. Namely, we penalize the Mutual Information between the goal and action or goal and skill (TBD the right way to do this).
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Ideally, this would allow goal-dependent skills, where the goal is not the entire state space. For example, penalizing Mutual Information could cause just the desired block position as the information to be passed to the skill. This ignores the irrelavant components of the state space for that skill. Another skill may focus on whether the window is locked / unlocked, etc.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Get rid of weird threshold / turn into MPC-ish. Currently, when planning, we must tune the value_threshold for when we pass control to goal-conditioned policy. To get 89 percent on pointmaze we used -10. Instead of using a threshold, we could instead just treat the goal-conditioned policy as another skill. Furthermore, they could be seen as our primitive actions i.e. during planning we take the next state as the immediate next state instead of just jumping to goal (which would obv always be taken).

I often hear this question come up amongst performance-driven developers, and for the longest time I could never get a straight answer as to why the stack was so much better? After a long foray into the inner workings of how memory allocation is actually done, I think I finally have an answer. I do not want to forget this, so I am doing a quick write up here.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
This all comes down to what happens during each memory allocation. Prior to actually running the program, the operating system allocates some amount of memory for both the stack and the heap (I think around 2-4MB?). When you allocate memory on the stack i.e. int x = 1;
Stack just increments stack pointer.
Writes value to new address pointed to by stack pointer. When you allocate memory on the heap i.e. int *x = malloc(sizeof(int)), we must instead choose how best to fulfill the request, which is a whole research direction in itself.
One such implementation is the buddy algorithm However, malloc itself is not a system call and therefore is not terribly slow. A real issue occurs when we run out of pre-allocated heap memory. This requires invoking a system call like sbrk to increment the size of the allocated memory for the heap.
If no available pages, OS must evict and write to disk...
Formally, this is known as "heap growth". Generally, if you know how much memory you need it is good practice to just allocated all up front to minimize any potential system calls. With this, the performance difference is not too drastic :)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Murphi is an explicit-state model checker: you describe a system as guarded transition rules, state the invariants, and it enumerates every reachable interleaving looking for a violation. That makes it a natural fit for cache coherence, where the steady-state behavior is easy and the races are not. This post builds a directory-based MESI protocol in Murphi, starting from MSI and adding state every time the checker finds a way to break it.

The state tables come from A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence, which doubles as the source for these notes. The recurring lesson is that the published tables are not quite enough: every protocol below needs transient states the tables leave implicit.
Syntactical things I need to remember from Murphi docs. Most things are straightforward, but there are a few things to note:
A declaration is a variable or a collection of variables that are used in the rules.
A rule is a transition from one state to another

html:ul.html:li: Each rule can optionally have an initial condition required to be fired
We can easily define rules for all the processors or collection of n things with ruleset.
For our use case, rules are used to define

html:ul.html:li: Must assign a value to every global variable

fr:mainmatter.html:p: An invariant is something that Murphi checks to ensure is true at all possible configurations of the system.

html:ol.html:li: Find all rules whose conditions are true in the current state. (i.e. conditional expressions are true, given the current values of the global variables).
Choose one arbitrarily and execute the action, yielding a new state.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The valid-invalid protocol shipped with the Murphi docs uses two Virtual Channels. A directory protocol needs three: one each for requests, forwarded requests, and responses. The reason is that deadlock is a cycle in the dependency graph, so it suffices to exhibit one.

html:ul.html:li: A node issues GetS to the directory, giving an edge N_1 \to D.
The directory forwards Fwd-GetS to the owner, extending the chain to N_1 \to D \to N_2.
The owner sends data back to the requester, closing the cycle N_1 \to D \to N_2 \to N_1.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The data closing that cycle would travel on the same channel as the requests waiting behind it, so a full request buffer wedges the response that would drain it. Partitioning by message class breaks the cycle:

html:ul.html:li: Request: GetS, GetM, PutS, PutM
Forwarded: Fwd-GetS, Fwd-GetM, Inv, PutAck
Response: Data, InvAck

fr:mainmatter.html:p: These are enumerated directly in the model's MessageType.
MESI is easier to reach through MSI, where there is less to get wrong and the races are already interesting enough.
The starting point is the primer's MSI cache controller table.

html:figure.html:figcaption: MSI cache controller. Rows are states, columns are events.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Several table entries are left blank; those are resolved at runtime from the AckCount, which is why the per-processor record carries an ack field alongside the state.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. load, store, and replacement only move the protocol between stable states. To simulate the system it is therefore enough to implement the rules that initiate those transitions — evict from modified, load from invalid — and let the model checker drive the transient states from there.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The directory side starts from the analogous table.

html:figure.html:figcaption: MSI directory controller.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: This table is where the first real gap shows up. It gives the directory a single transient state, and the races below force a second one, M^D.

fr:title.text: Losing data to a PutM/Fwd-GetM race

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Losing data to a PutM/Fwd-GetM race

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Consider the PutM rule that downgrades a cache from modified to invalid. The evicting cache must not drop the data when it sends PutM, because it may still have to service a forwarded request; it transitions to MI^A and keeps the value. But nothing stops the PutAck from arriving first, taking it to I before the Fwd-GetM shows up. The data is gone and the forwarded request has nobody to answer it.

Fix. Add the M^D state to the directory controller. While in M^D, a PutM from a node that is not the current owner stalls until the data arrives. Leaving M^D for M requires the new owner to send data back to the directory even on a three-hop transaction, so the directory learns that the forward actually completed. I have not found a cleaner way to close this race without the extra state.

fr:title.text: Deadlocking two stores against a load

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Deadlocking two stores against a load

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The M^D fix introduces a deadlock of its own. Take two processors that store-miss and a third that load-misses. The second store wins at the directory: the first store gets data and moves IM^{AD} \to IM^{A}, then the second triggers a Fwd-GetM that takes ownership away from it.

Meanwhile the load miss sits in IS^D. When its Inv arrives, the table says to stall — and because Inv and Fwd-GetM share the forwarded channel, that stall blocks the Fwd-GetM behind it. The winning processor never receives the data, and nothing ever drains the channel.

Fix. Another transient state absent from the table: II^A, meaning "was in IS^A, got invalidated, now waiting on PutAck before settling in I". The invalidation is processed rather than stalled, so the forwarded channel keeps moving.

fr:title.text: Not clearing the owner too eagerly

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Not clearing the owner too eagerly

fr:mainmatter.html:p: One more correction to the table: when the home directory is in M and receives a GetS, it must not clear the owner field as the figure directs. Once in S^D, the directory can no longer tell whether an incoming PutM came from the owner (and should stall) or from a stale node. The owner is only cleared once the data has actually arrived.
With those states in place the rest of MSI is mechanical, and MESI is a short step from it — modulo two design choices and two more races.

html:figure.html:figcaption: MESI cache controller.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Silent upgrades. If a cache in E may upgrade to M silently, the directory never learns the line went dirty, and the value it hands to the next GetS or GetM is stale. There are two consistent ways out: forbid the silent upgrade, in which case no forwarding is needed; or allow it and treat E exactly like M, forwarding everything. Neither requires a writeback on PutE. I take the first, matching the table.

Signaling exclusivity. The directory needs a way to tell a requester "you are the first reader, take the line exclusive." That is a new ExclusiveData message: receiving it in IS^D lands the cache in E rather than S. It turns out to also be the key to the second race below.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Once PutE or PutM has been sent, EI^A and MI^A are functionally identical. Both appear above for completeness, but transitioning from E straight into MI^A verifies the same.

html:figure.html:figcaption: MESI directory controller.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Symmetrically, the directory gains an E^D state, which for completeness is kept distinct from M^D but could be folded into it.

The first processor issues GetS and waits in IS^D, while the home directory has already moved to E and sent it ExclusiveData. A second processor then issues GetM, and home's Fwd-GetM overtakes the data in flight.
Fix. Stall Fwd-GetM and Fwd-GetS in IS^D until the data lands. This is safe here because the data is on the response channel, which no stall can block.

fr:title.text: Losing exclusive data to an invalidation

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Losing exclusive data to an invalidation

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The nastier version of the same race: the invalidation arrives before the forward. By the II^A rule inherited from MSI, a PutAck in that state drops the line to I — discarding data a forwarded request is about to ask for.

html:ol.html:li: Home takes the first GetS from Proc_1 → E, sends ExclusiveData
Proc_1 receives ExclusiveData → I, and the data is lost

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Fix. ExclusiveData pays for itself a second time. Because the message is distinguishable from ordinary Data, a cache receiving it in II^D knows it was the first reader and transitions to E instead of I — from which the pending Fwd-GetM or Fwd-GetS is handled correctly.
Folding all of the above in leaves these two state machines, which Murphi verifies exhaustively.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: This will be a brief tour through all the fundamentals needed to understand the first instantiation of FlashAttention as introduced in FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness.
This covers the math behind the online softmax algorithm required by Flash Attention (v1).
The first thing we must consider is numerical precision. Namely, the original softmax operation is given by
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: \mathrm {softmax}(\mathbf {x}) = \frac {\exp (\mathbf {x})}{\sum _{i=1}^n \exp (\mathbf {x}_i)}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: However, when operating with low precision data types (i.e. float16) the maximum value is 65536. Therefore, with \exp we can easily get numerically overflow.

To get around this, the online softmax algorithm adheres to the safe softmax. For safe softmax, we simply multiply the numerator and denominator by \exp (-m), where m = \max \{x_{1}, \ldots , x_n\}. This gives
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: \mathrm {softmax}(\mathbf {x}) = \frac {\exp (\mathbf {x} - m)}{\sum _{i=1}^n \exp (\mathbf {x}_i - m)}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Since x_i - m \leq 0, this ensures that each \exp (x_i - m) is bounded in a safe range.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. Note that computing the \max over \mathbf {x} means that we must have all of the logits in a row of QK^T materialized in SMEM, or first loop over all of them to compute the max before computing the normalization constant.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The online softmax algorithm fuses the max reduction into the normalization pass, so a single sweep over the row suffices to compute the normalization with the max. The key difficulty is that the denominator depends on n for each i i.e.
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: d = \sum _{i=1}^{n} \exp (x_i - m_n)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Therefore, we must find a recursive relationship such that d_{i+1} = f(d_i, m_i, x_{i+1}) for some function f. This would then allow us to locally compute d_{i+1} with only the local information of current x_{i+1} and the two running statistics d_i and m_i. This is exactly the kind of algorithm that is conducive to memory tiling.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Question. What is f(d_i, m_i, x_{i+1})?
Answer. Consider d_{i+1} = d_i \cdot \exp (m_{i} - m_{i + 1}) + \exp (x_{i + 1} - m_{i + 1}).

Proof. This can be seen by directly rewriting d_{i + 1}.
\begin {align*} d_{i + 1} &= \sum _{j = 1}^{i+1} \exp (x_j - m_{i + 1}) \\ &= \left (\sum _{j = 1}^{i} \exp (x_j - m_{i+1})\right ) + \exp (x_{i+1} - m_{i+1}) \\ &= \left (\sum _{j = 1}^{i} \exp (x_j - m_{i})\right )\exp (m_{i} - m_{i + 1}) + \exp (x_{i+1} - m_{i+1}) \\ &= d_{i} \exp (m_{i} - m_{i + 1}) + \exp (x_{i+1} - m_{i+1}) \end {align*}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The running denominator d is rescaled by e^{m - m_{\text {new}}} each time a new maximum is found, keeping it consistent with the safe-softmax shift.

html:pre.html:code: m = float("-inf") # running max of the logits d = 0.0 # running softmax denominator for i in range(n): # one fused sweep for the stats m_new = max(m, x[i]) d = d * exp(m - m_new) + exp(x[i] - m_new) m = m_new p = [exp(x[i] - m) / d for i in range(n)] # second pass: normalized probs

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Unfortunately, we cannot get around the second pass to compute the normalized output for \mathbf {p}. However, this is not the case in Flash Attention (v1).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Unlike in the online softmax, we are not interested in the outputted probability vector \mathbf {p}. Instead we are interested in the entire output matrix O given by
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: O = \mathrm {softmax}(QK^T) V
fr:mainmatter.html:p: For more details see self-attention.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Notation. In correspondence with the notation in the online softmax, we define the following: x_{i,j} = \mathbf {q}_i \cdot \mathbf {k}_j, where \mathbf {q}_i is the ith row of Q and \mathbf {k}_j is the jth row of K. Similarly, \mathbf {o}_i is the ith row of the output matrix O given by \mathbf {o}_i = \sum _{j = 1}^{n} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_n)}{d_n} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now following the template provided by the online softmax, we must find a recurrence for \mathbf {o}_i. Namely, we will consider the sequence \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' given by \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' = \sum _{j = 1}^{k} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j, such that \mathbf {o}_{i,n}' = \mathbf {o}_n
fr:mainmatter.html:div:
Claim. We have the following recurrence for \mathbf {o}_{i,k}':
\mathbf {o}_{i,k}' = \mathbf {o}_{i, k-1} \cdot \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k

Proof. We will proceed by directly rewriting the recurrence for \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' as

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The forward pass of flash attention avoids materializing the N \times N attention matrix by streaming an online softmax. The backward pass has to pull the same trick twice over, because the naive gradient computation wants two N \times N matrices — \mathbf {P} and d\mathbf {P}. Getting there means first writing down every gradient we need, then finding a way to recompute rather than store each one.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Notation. Following the notation in the original paper, \mathbf {S} = \mathbf {Q} \mathbf {K}^T, \quad \mathbf {P} = \mathrm {softmax}(\mathbf {S}), \quad \mathbf {O} = \mathbf {P} \mathbf {V}, where \mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, \mathbf {V}, \mathbf {O} are N \times d and \mathbf {S}, \mathbf {P} are N \times N. For a scalar loss \phi we abbreviate the gradient with respect to any matrix \mathbf {X} as d\mathbf {X} = \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {X}}, and write \mathbf {L}_i for the softmax denominator of row i saved by the forward pass, so that \mathbf {P}_{ij} = \exp (\mathbf {Q}_i \cdot \mathbf {K}_j) / \mathbf {L}_i.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Everything downstream is chain rule; the only step with any content is differentiating through the softmax. We take the gradients in dependency order, starting from d\mathbf {O} which arrives from the layer above.
Both fall straight out of the product rule for matrices:
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: d\mathbf {P} = \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {O}} \frac {\partial \mathbf {O}}{\partial \mathbf {P}} = d\mathbf {O} \mathbf {V}^T, \qquad d\mathbf {V} = \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {O}} \frac {\partial \mathbf {O}}{\partial \mathbf {V}} = \mathbf {P}^T d\mathbf {O}.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The shapes are a useful sanity check. d\mathbf {O} has one entry per output, so it is N \times d; \mathbf {V}^T is d \times N; their product is N \times N, matching \mathbf {P}. Likewise \mathbf {P}^T d\mathbf {O} is N \times d, matching \mathbf {V}.
Componentwise, from \mathbf {O}_{ik} = \sum _j \mathbf {P}_{ij} \mathbf {V}_{jk},
That last line is worth noting already: d\mathbf {V} never needs \mathbf {P} stored, only the ability to re-evaluate \mathbf {P}_{ij} from \mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, and \mathbf {L}.

Softmax acts row by row, so drop into the scalar case with \mathbf {s} and \mathbf {p} single rows. The softmax Jacobian is \partial \mathbf {p}_i / \partial \mathbf {s}_j = \mathbf {p}_i(\delta _{ij} - \mathbf {p}_j), giving

As a row vector this is d\mathbf {s} = \mathbf {p} \odot (d\mathbf {p} - \mathbf {p} \cdot d\mathbf {p}), where the subtracted term is the scalar \mathbf {p} \cdot d\mathbf {p} broadcast across the row. Collecting those scalars into a column \mathbf {D} with \mathbf {D}_i = \mathbf {P}_i \cdot d\mathbf {P}_i recovers the matrix form
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: d\mathbf {S} = \mathbf {P} \odot (d\mathbf {P} - \mathbf {D}).
fr:mainmatter.html:p: \mathbf {D} is the piece that will cause trouble later: it is a dot product over an entire row of \mathbf {P}, which is exactly the thing we refuse to materialize.
One more chain rule, and the sums run over opposite indices:

Every gradient above is expressed through \mathbf {P}_{ij} and d\mathbf {P}_{ij}, both N \times N. Materializing either one is exactly the quadratic memory cost the forward pass went to such lengths to avoid, so the backward pass has to be able to produce those entries on demand.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: 💡 Insight. Both are recoverable from the N \times d tensors already resident in memory. The forward pass saved \mathbf {L}, so \mathbf {P}_{ij} = \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}}, and d\mathbf {P} is just an inner product of two rows, d\mathbf {P}_{ij} = \sum _{k} d\mathbf {O}_{ik} \mathbf {V}_{jk} = d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {V}_j. Neither ever requires an N \times N intermediate.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Substituting both into the previous section leaves d\mathbf {Q} and d\mathbf {K} in terms of \mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, \mathbf {V}, d\mathbf {O}, \mathbf {L}, and \mathbf {D} alone:

One problem survives. \mathbf {D}_i = \mathbf {P}_i \cdot d\mathbf {P}_i is a dot product over a full row, so computing it inside the streaming loop would mean a reduction over all j before any tile of d\mathbf {Q}_i could be finished. This is the same global dependency the online softmax was designed to break.
The way out is that the row sum has already been computed once, in the forward pass. Expanding and pulling d\mathbf {O}_i out of the sum:

The inner sum is precisely the definition of \mathbf {O}_i. So \mathbf {D} is a single elementwise product of d\mathbf {O} and \mathbf {O} summed along the head dimension — one O(Nd) pass over tensors we already have, done once before the backward loop begins.
Forward pass. Store \mathbf {O} and the softmax denominators \mathbf {L}, both O(Nd).
Between the passes. Receive d\mathbf {O} from the layer above (automatic in JAX), then precompute \mathbf {D}_i = d\mathbf {O}_i \cdot \mathbf {O}_i in O(N) memory.
Backward pass. Stream over tiles, recomputing \mathbf {P}_{ij} from \mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, \mathbf {L} and d\mathbf {P}_{ij} from d\mathbf {O}, \mathbf {V} as needed:

html:ol.html:li: d\mathbf {V}_j = \sum _i \mathbf {P}_{ij} d\mathbf {O}_i, accumulated over query tiles.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Each accumulator is O(d) per row or column, so the whole backward pass stays linear in N.

This seems to be needed to ensure that the decoder cannot overfit to the offline data?
A termination network \beta _{\theta }(b_t \mid x_{1}, \ldots , x_{t})
A skill posterior \eta _{\theta }(z_{t} \mid z_{t - 1}, b_{t}, x_{1:T},a_{1:T}).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Unlike in DDO, where they do exact posterior inference, here we do variational inference. Namely, they directly try to model the posterior via the neural network \eta _{\theta }(z_{t} \mid z_{t - 1}, b_{t}, x_{1:T},a_{1:T}). This has a few consequences:

html:ul.html:li: The expectation gradient is now true Expectation Maximization. In particular, we need to optimize the ELBO.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The ELBO of LOVE can be written as
Notably this requires a few additional prior networks for the KL regularization term in the ELBO.

html:ul.html:li: A boundary prior \beta (b_t \mid s_{t}).
A skill prior p(z).
A state abstraction transition prior p(s_t | s_{t-1}, z_t).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Additionally, we also need to sample the z's. This is done via Gumbel softmax and causes much higher variance.

html:figure.html:figcaption: How LOVE goes from input sequence to end skill labels.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We find ourselves in-between LOVE and DDO. In particular, in DDO, they are concerned with learning a hierarchy of policies where the higher-level meta policy \eta must be usable online only given the current state.

html:ul.html:li: (+) The learned termination conditions \beta are dependent on the active skill.
(+) Exact inference \implies lower variance.
(-) Weak skill model \eta (z \mid s).
(-) No explicit encouragement for temporally-extended skills.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: On the contrary, in LOVE, they treat skills as a pure sequence-modeling problem. The posterior q_{\theta }(z_{t} \mid z_{t - 1}, b_{t}, x_{0}, \ldots , x_{T}) is purely used to label offline trajectories and give the skills meaning. To make them usable online, it is then required to learn an additional hierarchical policy over these skills.

html:ul.html:li: (+) The skill-labeler is allowed to use not only the current state but also the future visited states.
(+) Compression objective encourages temporally extended skills.
(-) Design inherently does not allow the terminations to be skill-dependent.
(-) Need to sample z's to compute gradients \implies higher-variance.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Our graphical model. We try to combine the desirable properties.

html:figure.html:figcaption: Each boundary depends on a skill and each skill depends on the whole sequence. Each boundary also depends on the whole history. However, the skill conditioned policy only requires the current state s and skill z. Thus, allowing the skills to be used.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We essentially combine the insight of LOVE where instead of trying to model the full joint distribution i.e. \mathbb {P}(\mathcal {H}, \xi ) we instead model \mathbb {P}(\mathcal {A}, \xi \mid \mathcal {S}), where we treat the entire state history as known.

In the language of HMMs, the emission probabilities only correspond to the actions. Therefore, we can perform the Forward-backward algorithm and condition on whatever component of the state we want without breaking the exactness.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. This is only a good idea for us because we do not need to use the meta controller during evaluation.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Deliberation cost. In LOVE, they encourage temporal extension through the compression loss. This requires an empirical approximation of the skillmarginal p(z). For me, this caused the skill entropy to just collapse to zero instead of encouraging temporally extended options. Instead, we use a deliberation cost more common in the options literature The Option-Critic Architecture, where we just add the switch-rate as an additional loss term.

html:ul.html:li: We are given the posterior \mathbb {P}(z_t = z, b_t = 1 \mid \mathcal {H}). In our implementation this would be (B, T, K)
We marginalize over skills z by summing to get \mathbb {P}(b_t = 1 \mid \mathcal {H})
Then average over batch B and time T to get expected reads.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: As in LOVE, we need to balance minimizing log-likelihood with compression / switching cost. To do so, we do dual descent.

html:ul.html:li: First, without compression, we run the algorithm and observe what is approximately the best attainable log-likelihood loss is.
Then, we minimize the deliberation cost subject to \mathcal {L}_{\text {likelihood}} \leq C + \epsilon
The skill network \eta (z_t \mid s_{0}, \ldots s_{T}) is a bidirectional GRU, where the hidden states are accumulated via running the GRU forwards and backwards and concatenating the results.
The termination network \beta (b_t \mid z_{t - 1}, s_{0}, \ldots , s_{t}) is a GRU, that only runs forward.
Instead of passing the previous skill as input, the output dimension is size K (number of skills).
The skill policy network \pi _{\theta }(a \mid s, z) is a standard Gaussian policy that take z as a one-hot encoding.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Setup. Assume we are given a set of skills \mathbf {z} \in \{0, \ldots , K\} along with a skill-conditioned lower-level policy \pi (s \mid z). Then what we want is to be able to learn the optimal goal-reaching policy over these skills. To do so, we must go beyond traditional offline skill-learning algorithms. We must Learn a value function over learned skills purely from offline data

Extending beyond pointmaze in locomotion. The main issue faced here is that our discriminator is too powerful in high dimensional state space. Namely, we score options based on their ability to reconstruct actions i.e. if \mathbb {P}(a_t \mid s_t, z_t = z) is high then we further increase the probability of selecting that option z. In higher-dimensional state spaces, the skill network \pi _{\theta }(a_t \cdot \mid s_t, z) is powerful enough to reconstruct a_t purely from s_t without using z. This basically provides no signal for which z to use, and we end up just selecting z uniformly every time step.

html:ul.html:li: I have seen a little sign of life from trying \pi (a \mid f_{\theta }(s), z) i.e. compressing s to a lower dimensional representation.
It may also be worth trying a really small network. Right now (256, 256) already gets very low reconstruction loss, so maybe we can go smaller?

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Conquering manipulation. In OGBench: Benchmarking Offline Goal-Conditioned RL, they provide a suite of manipulation environments in addition to the standard locomotion. One such environment, is the manipulation equivalent of the lights out game. This is a great test-bed to separate skill-learning from planning. In particular, the skill-learning portion can be clearly decomposed into the pressing of each of the buttons. However, when directly trying to use the LOVE it is not able to distinguish between these skills.

html:ul.html:li: On puzzle 3x3 LOVE terminates every 1.4 steps because all the skills look similar.
This is using the threshold \beta > 0.9.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pressing each of the buttons looks too similar, where the main discrepancy between them is only their termination condition. Since LOVE's termination condition is independent of skill, it is unable to distinguish between these.

html:ul.html:li: This is further confirmed in the scene environment. LOVE is able to distinguish between very different skills like open drawer vs. window. However, it is not able to distinguish between unlock drawer vs. window, where they only differ in pressing two adjacent buttons.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Injecting goals into the graphical model. Another failure mode of manipulation is that skills cannot be goal-independent. For example, in the generating policy of scene they have a pick and place skill that picks up the block and places it somewhere. Where to place the block is encoded in the goal. We can augment our graphical model to also allow the actions to depend on the goal.

html:figure.html:figcaption: Our graphical model with the goal included.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: However, we do not want the skills to become goal-conditioned policies. To get around this we can use the information bottleneck idea from InfoBot: Transfer and Exploration via the Information Bottleneck. Namely, we penalize the Mutual Information between the goal and action or goal and skill (TBD the right way to do this).
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Ideally, this would allow goal-dependent skills, where the goal is not the entire state space. For example, penalizing Mutual Information could cause just the desired block position as the information to be passed to the skill. This ignores the irrelavant components of the state space for that skill. Another skill may focus on whether the window is locked / unlocked, etc.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Get rid of weird threshold / turn into MPC-ish. Currently, when planning, we must tune the value_threshold for when we pass control to goal-conditioned policy. To get 89 percent on pointmaze we used -10. Instead of using a threshold, we could instead just treat the goal-conditioned policy as another skill. Furthermore, they could be seen as our primitive actions i.e. during planning we take the next state as the immediate next state instead of just jumping to goal (which would obv always be taken).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We find ourselves in-between LOVE and DDO. In particular, in DDO, they are concerned with learning a hierarchy of policies where the higher-level meta policy \eta must be usable online only given the current state.

html:ul.html:li: (+) The learned termination conditions \beta are dependent on the active skill.
(+) Exact inference \implies lower variance.
(-) Weak skill model \eta (z \mid s).
(-) No explicit encouragement for temporally-extended skills.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: On the contrary, in LOVE, they treat skills as a pure sequence-modeling problem. The posterior q_{\theta }(z_{t} \mid z_{t - 1}, b_{t}, x_{0}, \ldots , x_{T}) is purely used to label offline trajectories and give the skills meaning. To make them usable online, it is then required to learn an additional hierarchical policy over these skills.

html:ul.html:li: (+) The skill-labeler is allowed to use not only the current state but also the future visited states.
(+) Compression objective encourages temporally extended skills.
(-) Design inherently does not allow the terminations to be skill-dependent.
(-) Need to sample z's to compute gradients \implies higher-variance.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We essentially combine the insight of LOVE where instead of trying to model the full joint distribution i.e. \mathbb {P}(\mathcal {H}, \xi ) we instead model \mathbb {P}(\mathcal {A}, \xi \mid \mathcal {S}), where we treat the entire state history as known.

In the language of HMMs, the emission probabilities only correspond to the actions. Therefore, we can perform the Forward-backward algorithm and condition on whatever component of the state we want without breaking the exactness.

For me, this caused the skill entropy to just collapse to zero instead of encouraging temporally extended options. Instead, we use a deliberation cost more common in the options literature The Option-Critic Architecture, where we just add the switch-rate as an additional loss term.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: As in LOVE, we need to balance minimizing log-likelihood with compression / switching cost. To do so, we do dual descent.

Then, we minimize the deliberation cost subject to \mathcal {L}_{\text {likelihood}} \leq C + \epsilon
The skill network \eta (z_t \mid s_{0}, \ldots s_{T}) is a bidirectional GRU, where the hidden states are accumulated via running the GRU forwards and backwards and concatenating the results.
The termination network \beta (b_t \mid z_{t - 1}, s_{0}, \ldots , s_{t}) is a GRU, that only runs forward.
Instead of passing the previous skill as input, the output dimension is size K (number of skills).
The skill policy network \pi _{\theta }(a \mid s, z) is a standard Gaussian policy that take z as a one-hot encoding.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Setup. Assume we are given a set of skills \mathbf {z} \in \{0, \ldots , K\} along with a skill-conditioned lower-level policy \pi (s \mid z). Then what we want is to be able to learn the optimal goal-reaching policy over these skills. To do so, we must go beyond traditional offline skill-learning algorithms. We must Learn a value function over learned skills purely from offline data

Extending beyond pointmaze in locomotion. The main issue faced here is that our discriminator is too powerful in high dimensional state space. Namely, we score options based on their ability to reconstruct actions i.e. if \mathbb {P}(a_t \mid s_t, z_t = z) is high then we further increase the probability of selecting that option z. In higher-dimensional state spaces, the skill network \pi _{\theta }(a_t \cdot \mid s_t, z) is powerful enough to reconstruct a_t purely from s_t without using z. This basically provides no signal for which z to use, and we end up just selecting z uniformly every time step.

html:ul.html:li: I have seen a little sign of life from trying \pi (a \mid f_{\theta }(s), z) i.e. compressing s to a lower dimensional representation.
It may also be worth trying a really small network. Right now (256, 256) already gets very low reconstruction loss, so maybe we can go smaller?

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Conquering manipulation. In OGBench: Benchmarking Offline Goal-Conditioned RL, they provide a suite of manipulation environments in addition to the standard locomotion. One such environment, is the manipulation equivalent of the lights out game. This is a great test-bed to separate skill-learning from planning. In particular, the skill-learning portion can be clearly decomposed into the pressing of each of the buttons. However, when directly trying to use the LOVE it is not able to distinguish between these skills.

html:ul.html:li: On puzzle 3x3 LOVE terminates every 1.4 steps because all the skills look similar.
This is using the threshold \beta > 0.9.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pressing each of the buttons looks too similar, where the main discrepancy between them is only their termination condition. Since LOVE's termination condition is independent of skill, it is unable to distinguish between these.

html:ul.html:li: This is further confirmed in the scene environment. LOVE is able to distinguish between very different skills like open drawer vs. window. However, it is not able to distinguish between unlock drawer vs. window, where they only differ in pressing two adjacent buttons.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Injecting goals into the graphical model. Another failure mode of manipulation is that skills cannot be goal-independent. For example, in the generating policy of scene they have a pick and place skill that picks up the block and places it somewhere. Where to place the block is encoded in the goal. We can augment our graphical model to also allow the actions to depend on the goal.

html:figure.html:figcaption: Our graphical model with the goal included.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: However, we do not want the skills to become goal-conditioned policies. To get around this we can use the information bottleneck idea from InfoBot: Transfer and Exploration via the Information Bottleneck. Namely, we penalize the Mutual Information between the goal and action or goal and skill (TBD the right way to do this).
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Ideally, this would allow goal-dependent skills, where the goal is not the entire state space. For example, penalizing Mutual Information could cause just the desired block position as the information to be passed to the skill. This ignores the irrelavant components of the state space for that skill. Another skill may focus on whether the window is locked / unlocked, etc.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Get rid of weird threshold / turn into MPC-ish. Currently, when planning, we must tune the value_threshold for when we pass control to goal-conditioned policy. To get 89 percent on pointmaze we used -10. Instead of using a threshold, we could instead just treat the goal-conditioned policy as another skill. Furthermore, they could be seen as our primitive actions i.e. during planning we take the next state as the immediate next state instead of just jumping to goal (which would obv always be taken).

A hidden markov model is a statistical model, where the hidden states h \in \mathcal {H} form a Markov Chain, such that \mathbb {P}(h_{t+1} \mid h_{1}, \ldots , h_{t}) = \mathbb {P}(h_{t + 1} \mid h_{t})
Unlike a Markov chain, in addition to the hidden states, a hidden markov models contains observations x \in \mathcal {X} with associated emission probabilities \mathbb {P}(x_t \mid h_t).

html:figure.html:figcaption: Graphical model of a hidden markov model.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From the graphical model, we can see that for any i < j, (x_{0}, \ldots , x_i) \perp (x_{j}, \ldots , x_{N}) \mid z_{i}. Or in english, observations are independent conditioned on the hidden state.
Suppose we have a sequence of latent variable \xi = (z_{1}, z_{2}, \ldots , z_{T}) and the corresponding sequence of observations \mathcal {H} = (x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots , x_{T})
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Goal. We want to compute the posterior distribution \mathbb {P}(\xi \mid \mathcal {H}).
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Suppose \mathcal {z} is a discrete random variable taking at most K different values. Then, for horizon length T, there are K^T possible values for \xi . Thus, computing \mathbb {P}(\xi \mid \mathcal {H}) blows up exponentially.

html:div.html:p: Suppose that z \in \{0, 1\} and T = 2. Then

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Directly computing the probability for each possible value of \xi would thus take O(K^T) or exponential in the horizon length. Can we do better?
In the particular case of a hidden markov model, we can achieve O(TK^2)!!!

A hidden markov model is a statistical model, where the hidden states h \in \mathcal {H} form a Markov Chain, such that \mathbb {P}(h_{t+1} \mid h_{1}, \ldots , h_{t}) = \mathbb {P}(h_{t + 1} \mid h_{t})
Unlike a Markov chain, in addition to the hidden states, a hidden markov models contains observations x \in \mathcal {X} with associated emission probabilities \mathbb {P}(x_t \mid h_t).

html:figure.html:figcaption: Graphical model of a hidden markov model.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From the graphical model, we can see that for any i < j, (x_{0}, \ldots , x_i) \perp (x_{j}, \ldots , x_{N}) \mid z_{i}. Or in english, observations are independent conditioned on the hidden state.
In our setup, we can rewrite the marginal as
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: \mathbb {P}(z_t \mid \mathcal {H}) = \mathbb {P}(z_t \mid x_{0}, \ldots , x_{T})
fr:mainmatter.html:p: From Baye's rule, we can decompose this as
Since we are considering an HMM, (x_{1}, \ldots , x_t) and (x_{t + 1}, \ldots , x_{T}) are conditionally independent conditioned on z_t. Thus, we can further simplify this to
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: \mathbb {P}(z_t \mid x_{0}, \ldots , x_{T}) = \frac {\mathbb {P}(x_{t + 1}, \ldots , x_{T} \mid z_t) \mathbb {P}(x_{0}, \ldots , x_{t}, z_t)}{\mathbb {P}(x_{0}, \ldots , x_{T})}
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Notation. We will now consider the terms in the numerator separately. The first can be viewed as the backward term \beta _t(z) = \mathbb {P}(x_{t + 1}, \ldots , x_{T} \mid z_t = z), and the second as the forward term \phi _t(z) = \mathbb {P}(x_{0}, \ldots , x_{t}, z_t = z). Naming convention is to denote which direction in time information propagates (we will see shortly).
Remark. Both passes are O(TK^2) because at each timestep, it requires computing \mathbb {P}(z_{t} \mid z_{t - 1}) or \mathbb {P}(z_{t + 1} \mid z_{t}) which is a K \times K transition matrix.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Notably, the structure of the HMM ensures each marginal \mathbb {P}(z_t \mid \mathcal {H}) depends only on the local transition probabilities \mathbb {P}(z_{t} \mid z_{t - 1}) and \mathbb {P}(z_{t + 1} \mid z_{t}) rather than the exponential global \mathbb {P}(z_{0}, \ldots , z_{T}). This lends itself to the idea of a dynamic programming algorithm, where we compute the posterior of the preceding / succeeding latent and use the result for the next. Since we have bi-directional dependencies this requires making two passes a forward and backward pass. The key remaining detail is that these components can be efficiently combined to recover the full true marginal.
Finally, all that remains is to combine \phi and \beta to recover the true posterior. Recall that these directly correspond to the components in the numerator i.e.
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: \mathbb {P}(z_t \mid \mathcal {H}) = \frac {\phi _t(z) \beta _t(z)}{\mathbb {P}(\mathcal {H})}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Therefore, it remains to compute the normalization term \mathbb {P}(\mathcal {H}). To do so, note that
Thus, the true posterior can be recovered as
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: \mathbb {P}(z_t \mid \mathcal {H}) = \frac {\phi _t(z) \beta _t(z)}{\sum _{z} \phi _t(z)\beta _t(z)}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Since z is discrete, this sum is only O(K) and therefore easily computable.

The mutual information between two random variables X, Y is defined with respect to their joint distribution. Namely, it is the Kullback-Liebler Divergence between the joint distribution p(x,y) and the product of the marginals p(x)p(y) i.e. H(X || Y) = \mathbb {E}_{x,y \sim p(x,y)}\left [\log \frac {p(x, y)}{p(x)p(y)}\right ]
